title: India Will Play Twenty ODIs Before the 2027 World Cup. The Afghanistan Series Is Where the Rebuild Begins.
excerpt: With Kohli injured, Jadeja and Axar rested by design, and three uncapped players in the squad, Saturday's first ODI in Dharamsala marks the start of India's most deliberate white-ball reset in a decade
body:
On Saturday afternoon in Dharamsala, Shubman Gill will walk out for the toss with the snow-capped Dhauladhar range behind him and a question that extends far beyond three ODIs against Afghanistan: what does India's white-ball team look like when the World Cup is fourteen months away?

The answer will not arrive in a single series. But this is where the search begins.

The Numbers Tell the Story

India are scheduled to play roughly twenty ODIs before the 2027 Champions Trophy and ODI World Cup cycle reaches its peak. That is not a large number. Australia, England, and South Africa are each playing a comparable volume, and all of them are further along in their rebuilds. India's window for experimentation is narrow, which makes every squad selection between now and then a statement of intent.

The Afghanistan series is the first such statement. And it is louder than it might appear.

Virat Kohli is absent — a hamstring injury sustained during the IPL 2026 final for Royal Challengers Bengaluru ruled him out. In his place, Yashasvi Jaiswal has been called up. It is not just a replacement; it is a glimpse of what India's top order might look like in a post-Kohli future.

Jaiswal, who has demolished Test attacks with a technique built for all formats, slots in at number three in the predicted XI, behind Rohit Sharma and Gill.

The Deliberate Absences

The selectors have rested Ravindra Jadeja and Axar Patel for the series — not because they are injured, but because India want to test alternatives. This is a significant departure from recent practice. For years, India's ODI spin combination was settled. Now, with Kuldeep Yadav, Washington Sundar, and debutant Harsh Dubey in the squad, the selectors are asking whether there is a better configuration.

Dubey is the name to watch. The off-spinner was part of India's squad for the one-off Test against Afghanistan at Chandigarh but did not get a game — Manav Suthar played instead and took six wickets on debut. Now Dubey gets his chance in a different format. Former India all-rounder Abhishek Nayar, previewing the series for Star Sports, slotted Dubey at number eight in his predicted XI — a position that demands bowling control and lower-order batting composure.

Prince Yadav and Gurnoor Brar, the other two uncapped players in the squad, represent India's attempt to build bowling depth. With Mohammad Siraj rested for the concurrent tour of Ireland and England, and Jasprit Bumrah saved for the Asian Games, Prasidh Krishna and Arshdeep Singh will share the new ball. But it is the fringe players who will define whether this series achieves its developmental purpose.

Gill's Captaincy Audition Continues

Shubman Gill leads the side with Shreyas Iyer as his vice-captain. For Gill, this is not a new role — he captained India in the recently concluded Test against Afghanistan, where India won by an innings and 300 runs. But ODI captaincy is a different challenge, and the 2027 World Cup cycle will likely be defined by who leads India in the 50-over format.

Rohit Sharma is in the squad and will open the batting, but his role is evolving. At 39, he remains India's most experienced ODI campaigner, but the captaincy has shifted. The dynamic between Rohit as senior batter and Gill as captain will be one of the more closely watched subplots of this series.

Hardik Pandya, cleared by the BCCI Centre of Excellence after a back spasm during the IPL, returns as the primary all-rounder. He has not played an ODI in fifteen months. His fitness and form in the middle overs will be crucial to the balance India are trying to find.

The Schedule and the Stakes

The three ODIs are spread across three cities: Dharamsala on June 13, Lucknow on June 17, and Chennai on June 20 — all 1:30 PM IST starts, which means early morning for NRIs on the US East Coast and pre-dawn on the West Coast.

For the diaspora, the Afghanistan series may not carry the emotional charge of an India-Pakistan encounter or the prestige of an Ashes equivalent. But it is the kind of series that shapes World Cups. The players who succeed here will carry that confidence into the bigger assignments ahead. The combinations that work will become the template.

India's ODI rebuild does not begin with a bang. It begins with a toss at the foot of the Himalayas, against an opponent they just beat by an innings, in front of a crowd that will care deeply about what comes next.
